title: Fragrance Trends Decoded: What Consumer Search and Social Data Reveals About Scent Discovery
summary: Explore how TikTok, Google, and consumer behavior are transforming fragrance discovery. Uncover emerging scent trends, note preferences, and whitespace opportunities for bra
body_text: Ask someone under 30 how they found their last perfume. Chances are, it didn't start at a counter. It may have started with a TikTok, with some creator talking about a fragrance they're obsessed with, describing how it opens with bergamot and dries down into something smoky and warm. Then Google, checking the note breakdown on Fragrantica, reading three Reddit threads about whether it lasts. Then they bought it even without smelling it. And when the bottle showed up, they already knew what to expect because strangers on the internet described it so well that the first spray just confirmed what they'd already decided. But this model shouldn't work, because fragrance ought to be immune from online discovery, as you can't smell TikTok or sample a Google result. But instead, it's one of the categories most transformed by both. Understanding why it works anyway, and what consumers are actually searching for when they shop for their signature scents through a screen, is what separates the brands growing right now from the ones wondering where their customers went. How TikTok Changed Fragrance Discovery The Fragrance Community on TikTok PerfumeTok is one of TikTok’s largest and most commercially powerful beauty subcommunities. The hashtag #Perfume has surpassed 24B total views, while #PerfumeTikTok, #PerfumeTok, and #FragranceTok collectively account for billions more. The community produces an enormous volume of content: blind-buy reactions, layering tutorials, “smell like money” rankings, dupe comparisons, seasonal rotation tours, and “what perfume are you wearing” street interviews. A single video from the right creator can sell out a fragrance in days, and the comment sections function as focus groups where consumers tell you exactly what they want, what they’re searching for, and what they think of what they’ve already tried. The scale of this community matters because it has changed the power relations in the fragrance industry. Consumers used to discover perfume through advertising and sensory impressions in-store. Now they discover through content, recommendations, and social proof. A scent does not need a magazine ad or a celebrity face. It needs a creator who smells it on the camera and says something memorable about it. From Department Store to Algorithm: How Scent Is Being Discovered The department store counter isn’t dead, but it’s no longer where most fragrance discovery starts. Online fragrance sales rose in 2025, and the growth is being driven by consumers who arrive at the purchase already knowing what they want because they researched it online first. Before arriving at Sephora or ordering from an e-commerce site, they’ve made decisions, reducing purchase hesitation. This is because they've watched a TikTok review and read the note breakdown on Fragrantica. They’ve also compared three options on Google, so when they come in, a decision has already been made. This shift in the shopping journey is why search data has become so valuable for fragrance brands. The consumer’s path from interest to purchases now runs through algorithms on two major platforms: TikTok’s For You page creates awareness, and Google captures the purchase intent that follows. A brand that isn’t visible on both is missing half the story. But the brands that understand how to show up in both places, with the right content on TikTok and the right product information on Google, are the ones converting attention into sales. Dupes, Niche, and "Clean Girl" Aesthetics: The Search Behavior Behind Each Trend Three of the biggest fragrance trends on TikTok each generate distinct search patterns on Google. Dupes drive brand-versus-brand comparison queries: “Lattafa Khamrah vs Kilian Angels’ Share” or “best Baccarat Rouge dupe under $30.” The consumer already knows the reference scent. They’re searching for a cheaper version. Niche fragrance drives ingredient-led and note-led searches: “oud and amber perfume,” “sandalwood and musk fragrance,” “patchouli and vetiver cologne.” The consumer is thinking in terms of scent profile, not brand. The clean girl aesthetic drives function-adjacent queries: “light everyday perfume,” “scent that smells like clean skin,” “quiet luxury fragrance”. Each of these illustrates a different consumer mindset, and each requires a different content and product strategy to capture. The Fragrance Categories Generating the Most Consumer Interest Niche and Artisan Fragrance: Why Search Volume Keeps Growing Niche fragrance isn't small anymore; it's where the most interesting stuff in perfumery is happening, and consumers are following the journey. The person buying niche wants a scent that nobody else at dinner is wearing, which is the whole appeal: self-expression through what you smell like rather than what logo is on the bottle. Niche houses give their perfumers room to do things mainstream brands won't, like working with unusual materials, building compositions with multiple facets that shift over hours on skin, and using higher concentrations of oils that give a fragrance depth and sophistication. The result is something you can actually smell the difference in, and once a consumer experiences that difference, they rarely go back to the design. ​ The search data confirms what the market data suggests. Queries for niche fragrance brands and note-specific searches are gaining meaningful traction, and consumers are increasingly searching by scent profile rather than by brand name alone. They want to know what a perfume smells like at a molecular level: what the note composition is, how it evolves on skin, whether the dry-down is earthy or sweet or creamy or spicy. That specificity in search reflects a consumer who has become genuinely knowledgeable about perfumery, and it’s a consumer who rewards brands willing to tell a deeper story about what’s in the bottle. Oud, Amber, and Middle Eastern-Inspired Scents: A Sustained Breakout Oud didn't arrive in Western perfumery this year. It arrived on TikTok three years ago and never left. What started as creators reviewing $25 Lattafa bottles turned into a permanent change in what Western consumers expect perfume to smell like. Amber, musk, dark fruits like plum and cherry are the notes showing up alongside oud in search queries more than anything else, and they all point in the same direction. Warmer. Richer. More sensual. The fresh, citrus-forward scents that ran Western perfumery for years aren't disappearing, but they're no longer setting the pace. Brands like Lattafa, Arabiyat Prestige, and Kayali brought this scent family to Western consumers at accessible prices, and TikTok gave them the platform to do it at scale. What’s happening now is that luxury brands and established fragrance houses are responding with their own oud-forward and amber-heavy compositions, which tells you that the trend has moved from challenger brands into the mainstream market. The consumer who discovered oud through a $25 Lattafa blind buy is now exploring higher-end options, and their search behavior indicates it: queries are moving from “cheap oud perfume” to “best oud fragrance under $100” to “niche oud perfume” as their palate and budget evolve. Functional and Wellness Fragrance: Mood-First Scents Gaining Traction Something happened to fragrance that would have been hard to predict five years ago. People started shopping for scent the way they shop for supplements, based on what it does to their mood rather than what it smells like on a strip of paper. The search queries tell that story pretty clearly. "Perfume for focus and memory." "Calming scent for sleep." "Fragrance that reduces anxiety." This reads more like a wellness aisle than a perfume counter, but it's how a growing number of consumers describe what they want when they look for something new to wear. Hair perfumes fit into the same shift because they're not selling scent alone anymore; they're selling moisture, UV protection, and fragrance in one product, which is exactly the kind of multi-benefit positioning that this consumer responds to. Home scent and personal scent are also starting to overlap in interesting ways. Consumers who buy a specific candle want the matching perfume, or vice versa. Brands that build a scent universe across your body and your living space are tapping into something the search data suggests is growing, even if most fragrance houses haven't figured out how to do it yet. The full consumer data behind these shifts is explored in Spate's 2026 Fragrance Report . ​ The Brands Winning Fragrance Discovery Right Now How challenger brands are outperforming legacy houses in consumer attention Here's the part that would have been unthinkable a decade ago: the fragrance brands generating the most consumer attention in 2026 are mostly brands that Western shoppers hadn't heard of in 2021. They didn't outspend the competition because they couldn't; most of them didn't have the budget for a single magazine ad, let alone a global campaign. Most of them didn't have the budget for a traditional campaign. What they had was an understanding of how people actually find perfume now, which is through a creator's video rather than through the channels that used to dominate fragrance discovery. Building a brand around that reality from the beginning turned out to be an advantage that no amount of legacy marketing budget could reverse once the head start was established. Data from Market Defense shows that on Amazon, United Arab Emirates-based Lattafa leads the trend, crossing the $100 million sales mark on the platform during the last 12 months. Lattafa’s rise in US Amazon sales happened largely through TikTok creator content. Oakcha went all in on affordable gourmand and boozy vanilla compositions, put the product in front of TikTok creators, and then got out of the way. The audience discovered the brand on its own, which is the kind of organic growth that paid campaigns try to manufacture but rarely achieve. Kayali took a different path to the same outcome by positioning itself right where Middle Eastern scent traditions and Western consumer taste meet, building a line of fruity fragrances and warm compositions that are accessible enough for someone's first oud-adjacent purchase but interesting enough that they keep coming back. Legacy houses such as Chanel, Dior, and Tom Ford still command enormous market share and brand recognition. But they’re losing the discovery battle on social platforms because their content strategy is built within a world where a magazine ad and a department store counter were primary touch points. The consumer who discovers fragrance through TikTok wants authenticity, specificity, and access. They want to know what perfume smells like from a real person, not from a campaign. They want to understand notes, not just see the packaging. That’s a different set of customer demands, and the challenger brands are meeting them, while many legacy houses are still pondering how to adapt. What the data behind their growth reveals about consumer preferences The growth patterns of these challenger brands reveal several things about where consumer demand is heading. First, note-led discovery is replacing brand-led discovery. Consumers search for “vanilla and amber perfume” or “coffee and tea notes fragrance” before they search for a brand name. Second, the sparkling versus warm dynamic is shifting decisively toward warm. Searches for warm compositions, boozy accords, creamy sandalwood, nutty accords with almond and pistachio, and dark fruit notes like raspberry, berries, and plum are all outpacing fresh and citrus queries. What the challenger brands have in common tells you something about where the category is going. People are finding fragrance through scent profiles. Someone types "vanilla and amber perfume" or "coffee and tea notes fragrance" into Google and sees what comes up, and whoever matches that query best gets the click. The preference direction has moved warmer, too. Boozy vanilla, sandalwood with a creamy edge, almond and pistachio showing up in places they never used to, and dark fruits like raspberry and plum doing serious work in compositions that used to default to citrus or fresh aquatics. Those lighter profiles still sell and probably always will, but the energy in the category has moved somewhere warmer and heavier, and the brands riding that wave are the ones growing fastest right now. Third, consumers increasingly search for extrait de parfum over eau de toilette because they’ve learned that higher concentration means longer wear and better projection. The price conversation has also shifted. The idea that a perfume needs a hefty price tag to smell luxurious got dismantled publicly on TikTok, where $20 bottles routinely compete with $300 ones in side-by-side reviews. That doesn’t mean consumers won’t pay for luxury. It means they expect the scent to justify the price on its own, not lean on brand name or cosmetics-counter prestige. Where the Whitespace Is in Fragrance Demand clusters with no dominant brand positioned yet. Several fragrance opportunities are emerging where consumer curiosity is building, but branded supply hasn't caught up. Coffee and tea notes as primary accords are rising, according to fragrance industry experts cited by Who What Wear . The hot versus cold concept, fragrances that shift between warming and cooling sensations on skin, gets talked about constantly on TikTok, but almost nobody has actually built a product around it yet. Florals are in a similar spot where consumers got bored with straightforward rose and jasmine and started looking for blends that throw in vetiver or patchouli underneath to give the scent more weight and something to unfold into over a few hours. Wellness-positioned fragrance remains wide open. Scents marketed for focus, calm, or sleep using familiar ingredients like lavender, sandalwood, and bergamot ,but positioned as functional rather than purely aesthetic, sit in a gap between the wellness category and the perfumery category that very few brands have credibly filled. Hair perfumes as a format are growing in search, but the branded supply is thin beyond a handful of players. And the affordable niche space, artisan-quality compositions at accessible price points, continues to show strong consumer demand with room for new entrants who can deliver sophistication without the luxury price tag. For perfumers and fragrance brands watching these signals, the opportunity isn’t to chase every trending note. It’s to identify the demand clusters where consumer interest is real, growing, and not yet claimed by a dominant brand. Artificial intelligence is making this easier, with platforms that can sense shifts in search and social data weeks before they show up in sales. That’s where the whitespace sits, and where the next breakout fragrance brand will come from. For the full consumer data behind fragrance trends and emerging scent categories, download Spate’s 2026 Fragrance Report . FAQs ​How long does it usually take for a TikTok fragrance moment to turn into actual Google search volume? It varies and there's no fixed timeline because it depends on the category and the price point. A cheaper blind buy that goes viral is likely to generate Google searches faster than an expensive niche fragrance, where consumers want to research before committing. The useful thing about knowing that a gap exists at all is that it gives brands a window to position before the Google competition arrives, assuming they spotted the TikTok signal early enough. Should a fragrance brand put more resources into TikTok content or Google search optimization? Both serve completely different purposes and work best together. TikTok is where someone falls in love with a scent they've never smelled based on how a creator described it. Google is where purchase-intent queries for those same products tend to appear later. Investing only in TikTok generates excitement with no way to capture it at the purchase stage, and investing only in Google means ranking well for queries that are already crowded while missing the early signals about what consumers will be searching for next. Why do consumers search for notes and accords instead of brand names when shopping for fragrance? Because that's how they think about scent now. Five years ago, someone would search "Chanel perfume" and browse whatever came up. "In 2026, the more common query looks something like "warm vanilla amber evening fragrance" because the consumer already knows the scent profile they want and doesn't particularly care which brand makes it as long as the composition matches." For brands, this means your product page needs to contain the actual words consumers type, which are notes, accords, and occasions, not creative copy about a moonlit journey through a Moroccan garden. The brands ranking well in fragrance search right now are the ones whose product descriptions read like a Fragrantica entry rather than a poetry submission. What's the most reliable way to spot fragrance whitespace before a competitor fills it? You're looking for note combinations or formats where consumer search interest is climbing on both TikTok and Google, but no brand is owning the space yet. Coffee and tea as primary accords rather than background notes is one right now. Functional fragrance positioned around sleep or focus is another. The challenge is doing this manually because it means monitoring hundreds of search terms across two platforms every week, and will turn into a time-consuming task. That's the problem Spate was built to solve. We track these cross-platform signals and flag the gaps where consumer demand is rising faster than branded supply, which is exactly how you find the opening before someone else does. ‍

title: Retail & E-Commerce Tax Guide 2025
summary: Your 2025 tax playbook for retail & e-commerce. Master sales tax nexus post-Wayfair, inventory costing (LIFO/FIFO), and the new 1099-K thresholds.
body_text: 5. International Expansion Going global is a growth opportunity but it also invites a tangle of tax regimes, registration thresholds, and customs rules. Whether you're shipping physical goods abroad or offering digital products to overseas customers, international tax compliance is no longer optional. From navigating VAT and GST systems to understanding how Section 321 de minimis limits affect your fulfillment strategy, this section helps you manage risk and stay profitable as you scale internationally. For foundational differences between VAT and GST systems, see our full VAT vs. GST guide . 5.1 Import Duties & Section 321 De Minimis If you're shipping U.S. goods to international customers or importing products into the U.S. for resale, customs duties can eat into your margins quickly. Fortunately, Section 321 of the U.S. Tariff Act provides a major benefit for small shipments: Section 321 de minimis threshold: Allows duty-free import of shipments valued at $800 or less per day per recipient. Applies to B2C cross-border sellers who drop-ship from overseas warehouses (China, EU) to U.S. customers. Limitations: Must be a qualifying entry (one shipment per day per customer), and cannot be split to avoid duties. Certain restricted goods are excluded. For retailers using third-party fulfillment (e.g., Cainiao, SF Express, DHL eCommerce), it’s critical that your carrier is properly classifying the shipment under Section 321. Otherwise, duties and delays can pile up at the border. 5.2 VAT / GST Registration Thresholds (EU, UK, CA) Once you sell into foreign jurisdictions, you may need to register for VAT or GST and collect taxes at checkout. Unlike U.S. sales tax, these systems are destination-based and usually collected by the seller, not the buyer. Key registration thresholds: European Union (EU OSS): €10,000 in total intra-EU distance sales triggers VAT registration under the One Stop Shop (OSS) regime. File one return covering all EU member states. United Kingdom (UK): No threshold for non-UK sellers. If you sell goods shipped into the UK (or use UK fulfillment centers), you must register from your first sale. Canada (GST/HST): C$30,000 (approx. USD $22,000) annual threshold for non-resident digital or physical sellers. Above that, registration is required, and you must charge GST or HST depending on the province. 5.3 Cross-border Returns & Delivered-Duty-Paid (DDP) Models Returns and refunds become exponentially more complex in international commerce, especially when duties, taxes, and shipping fees are involved. Two primary fulfillment models determine your exposure: Delivered Duty Paid (DDP): Seller takes responsibility for all duties, taxes, and customs clearance. Improves customer experience but increases cost and complexity. DDP returns often require tax refund claims in the destination country. Delivered At Place (DAP): Buyer pays duties on arrival. Reduces seller burden but can lead to cart abandonment or failed delivery due to surprise costs. If you offer free returns, you must decide whether to absorb tax and duty losses or request refund documentation from customs authorities, a process that can take weeks and may require detailed paperwork. 5.4 Foreign Digital-Service Taxes & Marketplace Rules If you sell digital goods, subscriptions, or SaaS to international customers, many countries now impose digital services taxes (DSTs) or VAT-equivalent obligations on non-resident sellers. Key developments to track: EU & UK: Digital services (eBooks, online courses, SaaS) are subject to VAT at the buyer’s location — even if the seller has no presence in that country. Australia & New Zealand: Require immediate GST registration once threshold is hit and enforce compliance through platform reporting and penalties. India, Turkey, France, and Italy: Apply DSTs (2%–7.5%) on digital revenues from local users. While technically aimed at large tech platforms, enforcement may extend to mid-sized digital sellers. In many cases, marketplaces are deemed tax collectors under foreign law: Amazon UK and EU, for instance, are required to collect VAT for non-resident sellers shipping into their marketplaces. Etsy, eBay, and Shopify Markets have built-in VAT tools but you remain responsible for registering, reporting, and reconciling if you operate multichannel. 6. Payroll & Marketplace Reporting Retailers are now subject to a growing web of third-party reporting requirements and payroll-linked tax rules. From the shifting federal 1099-K thresholds to new state-level mandates and overlooked credits tied to in-store labor, these compliance layers affect your audit risk, staffing strategy, and tax refund potential. Let’s unpack what changed in 2025 and how to stay ahead. 6.1 1099-K Threshold Changes: The IRS’s planned enforcement of the $600 1099-K reporting threshold has been delayed again in 2025, but with a major adjustment: a $2,500 phased-in threshold now applies for the year. Here’s what that means: Who gets a 1099-K? Anyone who earns $2,500 or more in gross payments via third-party processors (Stripe, PayPal, Venmo, Amazon, Etsy, Shopify Payments) will receive a Form 1099-K for 2025. What’s reported? Gross transaction volume, not net of returns, fees, or shipping. Why it matters: Many casual sellers (especially on marketplaces) may now receive 1099-Ks for the first time, leading to confusion at tax time or duplicate income reporting if not properly reconciled. Action step for retailers: Match 1099-K totals to internal books, separating business vs. personal accounts. Educate small third-party vendors or dropship partners who may be unaware they’ll receive these forms. 6.2 State Marketplace Information Return Mandates Individual states are creating their own marketplace reporting obligations, often targeting marketplaces and payment platforms, but also affecting sellers who operate across multiple jurisdictions. Emerging trends: Colorado, Massachusetts, and California now require annual or quarterly information returns from platforms and, in some cases, sellers even if tax isn’t owed. Reporting includes seller identity, gross receipts by state, and product categories sold. Failure to file may trigger estimated assessments, sales tax notices, or withholding penalties even for compliant businesses. If you sell through Shopify, Amazon, or multi-channel apps, ensure your platform: Supports state-level reporting exports Separates taxable vs. exempt sales by destination Flags non-taxable channels to avoid overreporting Pro tip: Add a quarterly task to download your state-by-state gross receipts reports from each sales platform. Use these to preempt state notices and reconcile against your nexus exposure matrix. 6.3 ERC & Tip Credit Opportunities for Brick-and-Mortar Staff If you operate physical retail stores or hybrid models with in-person staff, don’t overlook payroll-linked tax credits still available in 2025: Employee Retention Credit (ERC), Still Amendable While new ERC claims are no longer allowed for 2021 and earlier, you can still file amended returns (Form 941-X) until April 15, 2025 (for 2021 Q1). Retailers hit by supply chain disruptions, reduced operating hours, or occupancy mandates in 2020–21 may still qualify even if revenue didn’t drop by 50%. Average credit: $5,000–$21,000 per employee, depending on eligible periods. Caution: Due to IRS backlog and fraud concerns, ERC audits have increased. Maintain payroll records, government mandate documentation, and revenue comparisons if claiming retroactively. FICA Tip Credit, Often Missed by Retailers If you operate restaurants, cafes, or retail locations where tipping occurs, you may be eligible for the FICA Tip Credit under § 45B. This credit offsets the employer’s share of Social Security and Medicare taxes paid on tips reported by employees, over and above minimum wage. Eligibility note: Employees must earn at least the federal minimum wage excluding tips for the credit to apply. Applies to both cash and credit-card tips. Action step: Coordinate with your payroll provider or CPA to ensure: Tip wages are properly classified and reported Eligible tip credits are applied at year-end or on quarterly returns 7. Tax Credits & Deductions While much of retail tax planning focuses on compliance and cost control, strategic use of tax credits and accelerated deductions can significantly reduce your federal and state tax liability. These incentives go beyond traditional manufacturing or tech sectors and many are tailor-made for retail, e-commerce, logistics, and hybrid businesses. Here’s how to unlock meaningful cash flow savings by tapping into underused credits and deductions in 2025. 7.1 R&D Credit for Custom Site and App Development Contrary to popular belief, the Research & Development (R&D) Tax Credit isn’t just for labs or biotech firms. If your retail or e-commerce business builds proprietary technology, including websites, shopping platforms, or custom integrations, you likely qualify for this powerful incentive. Key qualifying activities: Designing or coding custom e-commerce platforms, product configurators, or checkout workflows Developing mobile shopping apps, APIs, or integrations with payment or inventory systems Running A/B tests or UX optimizations involving technical experimentation Building logistics or fulfillment automation in-house See our full R&D Credit Guide to understand eligible expenses, recordkeeping tips, and how payroll R&D wages can reduce both income and payroll tax liability via Form 6765. 7.2 WOTC for Warehouse Hiring Retailers operating fulfillment centers or seasonal warehouses can benefit from the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC), a federal incentive that rewards hiring individuals from specific target groups. Eligible hires include: Long-term unemployed individuals SNAP (food stamp) recipients Formerly incarcerated individuals Qualified veterans and youth in designated zones Credit value : Up to $2,400–$9,600 per employee, depending on the category Claimed via Form 5884 after filing a pre-screening (IRS Form 8850) with your state workforce agency within 28 days of hiring Warehouse operations often attract candidates from WOTC-eligible populations but most retailers leave this credit unclaimed due to lack of screening processes. 7.3 § 179 Expensing & Bonus Depreciation for Fixtures and POS Hardware Upgrading your retail locations or fulfillment hubs? Tax law allows you to immediately deduct the cost of many capital improvements and assets under § 179 and bonus depreciation rules. Eligible assets include: POS systems and terminals Barcode scanners, mobile checkout devices, and receipt printers Display fixtures, shelving, and lighting installations Security systems and HVAC improvements § 179 (2025 limits): Up to $1.22 million in qualified asset purchases can be fully expensed (subject to income limitations) Phased out dollar-for-dollar once purchases exceed $3.05 million Bonus depreciation (2025): 60% of the remaining cost (after § 179) can be deducted immediately for qualifying new or used assets Tip : Use § 179 for smaller, income-limited entities; use bonus depreciation for large-scale investments or pass-throughs with enough income to absorb it. 7.4 Green Energy & EV Credits for Last-Mile Delivery Retailers investing in sustainable logistics or last-mile delivery may qualify for green energy tax credits, especially if deploying electric vehicles (EVs), solar charging stations, or alternative fuel infrastructure. Key opportunities: Commercial EV Tax Credit (45W) Up to $7,500–$40,000 per electric van, truck, or delivery vehicle Applies to new vehicles placed in service in 2023–2032 Credit amount depends on vehicle weight class and battery size Alternative Fuel Refueling Property Credit (30C) Up to $100,000 per location for EV chargers or hydrogen stations Must be installed in qualified census tracts (low-income or non-urban areas) State incentives: Many states offer stackable credits or rebates for EV fleets (e.g., California’s HVIP, New York’s NYTVIP) Bonus deduction: Solar panels, battery storage, and rooftop energy systems installed at warehouses or retail sites may qualify for Section 179D deductions or energy investment tax credits (ITC). 8. Risk Management & Audit Triggers Retail tax audits result from inconsistent filings, mismatched data, or exposure you didn’t even know you had. Managing audit risk in 2025 means identifying and addressing the red flags before a state revenue agency or the IRS does. 8.1 Common Nexus-Audit Flags As nexus rules continue to evolve post- Wayfair , tax authorities are increasingly using data analytics to flag businesses that appear to have exposure but aren’t filing. Here are common triggers for nexus-based audits : Marketplace + website combo: You sell through Amazon (where tax is remitted) and your own Shopify store (where it’s not), but only report Amazon sales. Inventory-based nexus: Using FBA or WFS creates physical presence in dozens of states. If those states don’t see registration, they may initiate a desk audit. Affiliate or marketing presence: Paying local influencers or running geo-targeted ads may create economic nexus (or even agency nexus), especially in California and New York. Threshold breaches without registration: Once a state’s sales threshold is crossed and no return is filed, your account may be flagged automatically for audit review. 8.2 False-Positive Fraud Filters (ZIP mis-mapping) One of the most overlooked audit risks is not fraud but false-positive fraud flags caused by bad address data. Most tax engines use ZIP code–based mapping to apply local tax rates, but in edge cases, ZIP boundaries don’t match jurisdiction boundaries. Here are a few examples: Denver, CO: Parts of ZIP 80210 fall inside and outside city limits — tax overcollection or undercollection is common. Chicago, IL and LA, CA: Nested districts with transit or local add-ons can cause incorrect local tax rates to apply if address data is too broad. Why this matters: Overcollection can trigger customer complaints and refund liabilities. Undercollection leads to remittance gaps, especially when states cross-check seller data with shipping destinations. Mitigation strategy: Use geolocation tax APIs (e.g., based on rooftop coordinates) instead of ZIP-only rules. Flag high-risk ZIPs where boundaries cross jurisdictions and test invoices regularly in those zones. 8.3 Record-retention matrix: what to keep and for how long Document Type Minimum Retention Why It Matters Sales invoices 6–7 years Verifies tax collected and product classification Exemption certificates Until statute ends (varies by state, typically 4–7 years) Required to justify exempt sales Shipping/fulfillment logs 4+ years Proves destination state for sourcing rules Tax returns & workpapers 7 years Supports reported figures and audit defense 1099-K and marketplace reports 4–6 years Reconciliation support, especially for hybrid sellers 8.4 Voluntary Disclosure Agreements (VDAs) & Amnesty Windows If you discover that you’ve had nexus or tax exposure in a state for years but never registered or filed, don’t panic, you may qualify for a Voluntary Disclosure Agreement (VDA). What is a VDA? A legal agreement between a business and a state where the business agrees to register and pay back taxes for a limited lookback period (usually 3–4 years). In return, the state waives penalties and doesn’t audit prior periods. When to consider a VDA: You used FBA or WFS and only now realized you created nexus in states like TX, PA, or IL. You exceeded a state’s economic threshold in 2022 but never registered or filed. You’re preparing for a merger, investment, or sale and want to clean up exposure. Amnesty programs : Some states periodically offer short-term tax amnesty windows that go even further, waiving penalties and interest, but they’re time-sensitive and less common. How to initiate: Work through a CPA, legal advisor, or third-party provider. States often allow anonymous inquiries so you can explore options before disclosing your identity. 9. Year-End Controller Checklist Whether you’re running a lean in-house team or managing multiple locations and channels, this checklist helps ensure your year-end process is both airtight and opportunity-aware. 9.1 Reconcile Sales-Tax Liability to General Ledger (GL) Start by matching your sales tax payable accounts to your actual liability across states. Key steps: Aggregate monthly tax collected per state from POS/gateway reports (Shopify, Stripe, Amazon, etc.). Reconcile to GL balances and filed returns, discrepancies often arise from: Manual journal entries for prior period adjustments Timing gaps between collection and remittance Returns or discounts improperly netted Tip: Create a summary sheet that shows tax collected vs. tax remitted by jurisdiction to flag any over- or under-payments. This not only supports audit readiness but also helps refine your filing cadence. 9.2 Close Inventory & Apply § 263a Capitalization (Including LIFO Review) As part of year-end financial prep, inventory must be closed accurately. Steps include: Inventory count & valuation: Conduct a physical count or confirm perpetual inventory reconciliation. Apply § 263A capitalization rules (if applicable): Capitalize indirect costs such as purchasing, storage, and handling onto ending inventory if not exempt under the § 471(c) safe harbor . LIFO vs. FIFO review: If using LIFO, assess for LIFO liquidation risk, where reduced year-end inventory levels trigger recapture of older, lower-cost layers, increasing taxable income. Strategy tip: If LIFO liquidation is unavoidable, consider offsetting gains with year-end bonus depreciation or accrued expenses. 9.3 Issue 1099-NEC to Influencers & Contractors If you’ve hired influencers, freelance creatives, or third-party marketing consultants in 2025, the IRS requires you to issue Form 1099-NEC if you paid them $600 or more and they’re not classified as employees. Year-end tasks: Collect W-9s before issuing payments, you’ll need legal names and TINs. Issue Form 1099-NEC by Jan 31, 2026. File copies with the IRS and applicable states, especially those that participate in the Combined Federal/State Filing Program. Common 1099-NEC recipients in retail/ecommerce: Influencers (paid for product promotion or content) Freelance developers, designers, and copywriters Independent warehouse workers or pick-pack contractors Affiliate marketers (if paid outside a platform) Risk alert: Failing to issue 1099s can result in $60–$310 penalties per form, plus potential audits of your classification policies. 9.4 Multistate Estimated Income-Tax Payments If your retail operations generate income across multiple states, due to inventory, payroll, or economic nexus, you may be required to make estimated state income-tax payments. Key tasks: Review your apportionment factors to project in-state income accurately Calculate Q4 state estimates due by Jan 15, 2026, or earlier for certain fiscal-year entities Account for non-conforming states (like CA, NY, and NJ) that do not fully align with federal tax timing or calculation rules 9.5 Verify Str / Lodging-Sales-Tax Filings (Where Applicable) If your business includes short-term rentals (STRs), pop-up shops, or lodging services, don’t overlook local lodging or occupancy tax requirements. Checklist: Confirm monthly or quarterly STR filings in platforms like Airbnb, Vrbo, or Booking.com haven’t missed any jurisdictions. For direct-booking sites, ensure sales tax, lodging tax, and tourism levies are properly separated on invoices. Some cities (e.g., NYC, Chicago, Miami) require local registration and tax returns, even if you're already filing state sales tax. Pro tip: Double-check venue bookings for Q4 activations (e.g., holiday pop-ups, event-based lodging) to ensure tax treatment is consistent with local STR rules. FAQs 1. Is shipping taxable in all states, or only if the product is taxable? Shipping taxability depends on the state and how the invoice is structured. In over 25 states, if the underlying product is taxable, the shipping charge is too. Some states also tax handling or combine it with shipping, making the entire amount taxable. To avoid overcharging customers, separate shipping and handling line items and ensure your tax engine or POS software accurately tags shipping based on each state’s rules. 2. How do I stay sales-tax compliant if I sell on Shopify and other platforms? Shopify sellers are responsible for collecting the correct tax across all states where they have nexus. While Shopify offers automatic tax collection tools, it doesn't handle registration or filing. Multi-channel sellers must consolidate marketplace vs. direct sales, ensure product tax codes are accurate, and file separate returns where needed. Shopify doesn’t file for you, it’s your responsibility to stay compliant with each state’s thresholds and filing requirements. 3. When do I need to register for sales tax due to economic nexus? Most states require registration once you cross their economic nexus threshold, typically $100,000 in sales or 200 transactions annually (though some states have removed the transaction count rule). Timing is key: you’re expected to register as soon as you exceed the threshold, not at year-end. Failing to register promptly can lead to penalties, back taxes, and interest. Keep a monthly nexus tracking log to catch exposure early. 4. Do I need to collect sales tax if I only sell digital products? Yes, in many states, digital products like eBooks, downloadable music, and SaaS subscriptions are taxable. Over 30 states impose tax on digital goods, and each has different rules. For example, a state may exempt eBooks but tax streaming subscriptions. If you sell digital products through Shopify or another platform, assign the right product tax code to avoid undercharging or overcollecting tax on those items. 5. Does Shopify collect and remit sales tax automatically for every state? No. Shopify collects tax based on your setup, but it doesn’t remit the tax to states or register your business. You must configure collection settings for each nexus state, assign accurate tax codes to your products, and file returns yourself (or through a provider). If you rely on marketplaces like Amazon that collect for you, keep those separate from Shopify direct sales to avoid double-counting or missing obligations. 6. What happens if I use Amazon FBA or WFS but don’t register in all warehouse states? If your inventory is stored in an FBA or Walmart Fulfillment Services warehouse, you likely have physical nexus in that state. Not registering can lead to tax notices or audits. Even if Amazon collects tax on your behalf, you may still need to register and file zero-dollar returns in warehouse states. Tools like the Amazon Inventory Event Detail Report can help map where you have physical nexus exposure. 7. How should I handle sales tax for orders that include both taxable and exempt items with shipping? In most states, when shipping is bundled with taxable and exempt products, tax must be prorated. If not, you risk either overcharging or undercharging tax. For example, a tax engine should calculate tax on 60% of the shipping charge if 60% of the order is taxable. Always separate items and use an invoicing system that applies shipping rules based on item taxability and the buyer’s location. 8. What are common sales tax mistakes Shopify sellers make during Q4? The busiest retail season often leads to compliance lapses. Common Q4 mistakes include: Missing new economic nexus thresholds due to year-end sales spikes Failing to update shipping tax rules for gift bundles or promotions Overlooking marketplace vs. direct-channel split when filing returns Not issuing or renewing exemption certificates for B2B buyers Use Shopify’s reports + third-party tax software to reconcile collected vs. remitted tax before year-end.

title: Lands’ End Announces First Quarter Fiscal 2026 Results
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Lands' End, Inc.'s business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: DODGEVILLE, Wis., June 09, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lands’ End, Inc. (NASDAQ: LE) today announced financial results for the first quarter ended May 1, 2026. Andrew McLean, Chief Executive Officer, stated, “Our first quarter results reflect a business with real underlying momentum. Consumer traffic was up double digits, new customer acquisition improved, and our European business delivered strong double-digit revenue growth — confirmation that our solutions-based strategy is resonating with customers. We experienced a temporary operational disruption tied to our U.S. distribution center upgrades which caused a timing issue, and it is behind us. Additionally, we delivered year-over-year improvement in both adjusted net income and adjusted earnings per share.” McLean continued, “Looking forward, the creation of the joint venture with WHP Global marked a genuine inflection point for Lands’ End and positions us to deliver outstanding shareholder value. Whether from the continued growth of our existing commercial operations, a much more favorable capital structure with no term-loan debt, the Board’s April authorization of a $100 million share repurchase program, the profit-share we’ll receive from the JV or the potential exchange of our JV stake into equity in WHP Global at the same multiple WHP receives in a qualifying monetization event, the opportunity in front of Lands' End has never been clearer, and we are committed to building on our successes and focused on delivering on the potential in this great American company.” First Quarter Financial Highlights Net revenue was $238.9 million for the first quarter of 2026, a decrease of $22.3 million or 8.5% from $261.2 million during the first quarter of 2025. The decrease in revenue was driven primarily by the temporary disruption associated with the rollout of a new warehouse management system and the deliberate pacing of shipments as the distribution centers ramped back to normal capacity. Excluding the impact of the temporary disruption, the Company estimates it would have delivered low single-digit revenue growth in the quarter. U.S. Digital Segment Net revenue was $205.1 million for the first quarter of 2026, a decrease of $22.6 million or 9.9% from $227.7 million in the first quarter of 2025. U.S. eCommerce Net revenue was $153.3 million, a decrease of $17.4 million or 10.2% from $170.7 million in the first quarter of 2025. The decrease was driven by the temporary disruption associated with the rollout of the new warehouse management system and the deliberate pacing of shipments as the Company ramped its distribution centers back to normal capacity. Outfitters Net revenue was $38.5 million for the first quarter of 2026, a decrease of $4.4 million or 10.3% from $42.9 million in the first quarter of 2025. The decrease was driven by the temporary disruption of the new warehouse management system. Customer orders from the business uniform channel remained strong primarily driven by select enterprise accounts. Third Party Net revenue was $13.3 million, for the first quarter of 2026, a decrease of $0.8 million or 5.7% from $14.1 million during the first quarter of 2025. The decrease was primarily due to a strategic focus on higher-margin, higher-quality sales, prioritizing brand integrity over lower-value, promotion-driven volume. Europe eCommerce Net revenue was $20.5 million for the first quarter of 2026, an increase of $2.6 million or 14.5%, from $17.9 million during the first quarter of 2025. The increase was primarily due to strategic shift to a franchise-first assortment simplifying the business and improving inventory efficiency. Gross profit was $111.5 million for the first quarter of 2026, a decrease of $21.2 million or 16.0% from $132.7 million during the first quarter of 2025. Gross margin decreased approximately 410 basis points to 46.7% in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 50.8% in the first quarter of 2025. The gross margin decrease was primarily driven by the deleverage created by the temporary distribution center disruption, the new royalty structure associated with the WHP Global JV and continued tariff headwinds. Selling and administrative expenses increased $3.0 million to $126.5 million or 53.0% of Net revenue in the first quarter of 2026, compared with $123.5 million or 47.3% of Net revenue in the first quarter of 2025. The approximately 570 basis point increase was driven by deleverage from lower net revenue and investment in digital marketing focused on new customer acquisition. Net income was $330.7 million, or $10.56 earnings per diluted share first quarter of 2026 compared to Net loss of $8.3 million or $0.27 loss per diluted share in the first quarter of 2025. The Net income result was primarily driven by the WHP Global transaction. Adjusted net loss was $3.5 million and Adjusted diluted loss per share was $0.11 in the first quarter of 2026, compared to Adjusted net loss of $5.4 million and Adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.18 in the first quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA was $(6.2) million in the first quarter of 2026, a decrease of 165% compared to $9.5 million in the first quarter of 2025. Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Highlights Cash and cash equivalents were $23.1 million as of May 1, 2026, compared to $18.1 million as of May 2, 2025. Inventories were $299.9 million as of May 1, 2026, and $262.4 million as of May 2, 2025, representing a 14% year over year increase. That increase primarily reflects the timing effects of the distribution center ramp-up and the unmitigated impact of tariffs. As operations normalize and inventory flow improves, the Company expects inventory levels to become better aligned with the Company’s revenue trajectory. Net cash used in operating activities was $74.2 million for the 13 weeks ended May 1, 2026, compared to net cash used in operating activities of $22.5 million for the 13 weeks ended May 2, 2025. The increase in net cash used in operating activities was primarily due to the impact of the closing of the WHP Global transaction and partially offset by increased inventory related to the temporary distribution center disruption. As previously announced, the Company used the majority of the $300 million in cash proceeds from the WHP Global transaction to fully repay its term loan. As of May 1, 2026, the Company had $30.0 million of borrowings outstanding and $104.2 million of availability under its ABL Facility, compared to $40.0 million of borrowings and $86.8 million of availability as of May 2, 2025. During the first quarter of 2026, the Company repurchased $0.3 million of the Company’s common stock under the share repurchase program announced on April 1, 2026. As of May 1, 2026, additional purchases of up to $99.7 million could be made under the current program through March 31, 2029. Outlook Bernie McCracken, Chief Financial Officer, stated, “Our first quarter financials reflect three distinct factors: the temporary disruption from our distribution center upgrade, structural P&L changes following the WHP Global transaction, and continued tariff pressure. Absent the operational disruption, we estimate we would have delivered low-single-digit revenue growth. In Europe, where distribution was not affected, revenue grew 15% and gross margin expanded approximately 70 basis points — evidence of the underlying health of the business.” McCracken continued, “The full repayment of our term loan has significantly strengthened our balance sheet and reduced our interest burden. Importantly, this step provides enhanced financial flexibility to capital allocation, including reinvestment in the business and returning capital to shareholders.” The Company’s guidance reflects current conditions, including tariffs at currently implemented rates and prevailing macroeconomic factors. For Second Quarter fiscal 2026 the Company expects: Net revenue to be between $290.0 million and $310.0 million. Net loss to be between $5.0 million and $2.0 million and diluted loss per share to be between $0.16 and $0.06 Adjusted net income to be between $2.0 million and $5.0 million and Adjusted diluted earnings per share to be between $0.06 and $0.16. Adjusted EBITDA in the range of $11.0 million to $14.0 million. For fiscal 2026 the Company now expects: Net revenue to be between $1.30 billion and $1.40 billion. Net income to be between $310.0 million and $320.0 million and diluted earnings per share to be between $10.02 and $10.34. Adjusted net income to be between $10.0 million and $20.0 million and Adjusted diluted earnings per share to be between $0.32 and $0.65. Adjusted EBITDA in the range of $68.0 million to $78.0 million. For the full year, the Company’s guidance includes approximately $40.0 million of capital expenditures. The enhanced earnings conference call will also include discussion of the Company’s strategy following the closing of its joint venture transaction with WHP Global and the potential value creation opportunities from that transaction. The call may be accessed through the Investor Relations section of the Company’s website at http://investors.landsend.com. About Lands’ End, Inc. Lands’ End, Inc. Lands’ End offers products online at www.landsend.com , through third-party distribution channels and our own Company Operated stores. Lands’ End also offers products to businesses and schools, for their employees and students, through the Outfitters distribution channel.
